title: How to Plan for Retirement if You Expect to Work Part-Time After 65
description: Integrating 'Active Income' into the withdrawal phase.
content:
Retirement is being redefined. For many, it's not the end of work, but the end of *required* work. Continuing to work part-time after age 65 (Phased Retirement) transforms the math of financial independence. By covering your basic bills with a light workload, you allow your portfolio to grow untouched for extra years, drastically increasing the probability of it lasting to age 100. This guide explains the tax, Social Security, and Medicare implications of working past 65.

Key Takeaways

  • Portfolio Preservation: Earning $25,000/year allows you to leave $625,000 of investments untouched (based on the 4% rule). Your labor is a massive asset.
  • Social Security Freedom: Income allows you to delay Social Security until age 70. This boosts your benefit by 8% per year, creating a larger inflation-protected floor for later life.
  • Medicare Interaction: If you work for a small company (<20 employees), Medicare is primary. If large (>20), employer insurance is primary. You can often delay Medicare Part B premiums if you keep employer coverage.
  • The 'Earnings Test' is Gone: Once you reach Full Retirement Age (66/67), the Social Security earnings test vanishes. You can earn $1 Million/year and still collect your full Social Security check.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 'Earnings Test' only applies if you claim Social Security early (62-66). It withholds $1 for every $2 earned above ~$22k. Waiting until FRA eliminates this penalty entirely.

The 'Barista FIRE' Math

Scenario: You need $60,000/year to live.

Option A: Full Stop at 65

Portfolio Withdrawal: $60,000.
Required Nest Egg: $1.5 Million.

Option B: Work until 70 ($30k/yr)

Work Income: $30,000.
Portfolio Withdrawal: $30,000.
Required Nest Egg: $750,000.
Impact: You can retire with half the savings just by working a fun, low-stress job for 5 extra years.

The Compounding Bonus

Because you aren't withdrawing $60k/yr, your portfolio likely grows from $750k to $1M+ during those 5 years. You end up richer at 70 than you were at 65.

Optimizing the Phase-Down

  1. Roth Contributions: Since you have 'Earned Income', you can still contribute to a Roth IRA at age 68. This is a great way to move money into tax-free status.
  2. HSA Eligibility: If you are on Medicare, you cannot contribute to an HSA anymore, even if working. Stop HSA contributions the month you enroll in Part A.
  3. Consulting vs W-2: Consulting (1099) allows you to open a Solo 401(k) and deduct business expenses. It is often more tax-efficient than a W-2 part-time job.
  4. RMD Management: If you work for a company and don't own >5% of it, you can delay RMDs from that specific plan until you actually retire (even if over 73). This is the 'Still Working' exception.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will I pay higher taxes?

Maybe. Earnings + Social Security + RMDs can push you into a higher bracket. Watch out for IRMAA (Medicare Surcharges). You might need to use Roth withdrawals to keep taxable income down.

What if I get fired?

That is the risk. You need a 'Plan B' budget that works without the job income. Ensure your portfolio can support a 'Lean' lifestyle if the work dries up.

Can I collect SS while working?

Yes. After FRA (67), there is no penalty. You get the paycheck plus the government check. It is a double-income stream.
